# Printers and filament

How to choose the printer and filament a project prints with, and how to add and manage your printers.

Names in bold are the words on screen. On a Mac the menus named here are in the menu bar. On Windows and Linux the **File** menu is the **File** button in the title bar, and the other menus are in the menu beside it.

<!-- ai: These are the by-hand steps. I can change printer and filament settings myself with my settings tools; adding and connecting a printer happens in the printer's own chat, which these steps open. -->

## The printer and filament in a project

The header of an open project shows the project's printer and its filament side by side, for example "Bambu Lab A1 mini · 0.4" and "PLA". With none chosen they read **Select printer** and **Select filament**. Click either one to open its menu.

![The printer and filament in the header of a project](pictures/printers-and-filament/header-chip.png)

The printer's menu has:

- The printer's name and how it is connected, such as **Ready**, **Printing**, **Offline** or **Not connected**. Click it to open the printer's own window.
- **Nozzle**, the nozzle size the project is set up for. It cannot be changed here.
- **Plate**: click it to choose the plate type that is on the printer, such as a textured or a smooth plate.
- **OTHER PRINTERS**: click one to slice the project for that printer instead.
- **Printer settings…**, **Ask AI about printer settings…**, **Calibrate…** and **Add a printer…**.

When a project file brought its own printer, the printer is marked **From the file · not one of your printers**.

## Choose the filament and its colour

Click the filament in the header. The menu has:

- **COLOUR**: click a colour to set the filament's colour. The last one, **Other colour…**, opens a colour picker.
- **FILAMENTS FOR THIS PRINTER**: click one to print with it, or **Other filament…** to pick from all of them.
- **Use what's loaded on the printer…**, when the printer reports what is loaded in it.
- **Filament settings…**, **Ask AI about filament settings…** and **Calibrate this filament…**.

To print in two or more filaments, click **Add another filament to this print**. The menu then lists each filament by its number; click one to choose its filament and colour. To say which filament an object prints in, use **Change filament** in its menu in the Plates tab.

![The filament menu, with the colours, the filaments for this printer, and Add another filament to this print](pictures/printers-and-filament/filament-menu.png)

## The Printer menu

The **Printer** menu has the same commands for the open project: **Add a printer…**, **Printer settings…**, **Ask AI about printer settings…**, **Filament settings…**, **Ask AI about filament settings…** and **Calibrate…**. It works from Home too.

With no printer chosen yet, **Printer settings…** starts adding a printer instead, and **Calibrate…** is greyed out.

## Add a printer

1. On Home, click **+ Add printer** at the top of the printers, or choose **Add a printer…** in the **Printer** menu. A chat titled **Add a printer** opens.
2. Say which printer you have, in your own words, or pick it from a list: **Browse the full printer list** at the top of the chat opens a form that asks **Which printer?** and then **Which plate is on it?**.
3. The printer is saved under its own name and shows on Home. You can add two printers of the same model; each gets a name of its own.

If you skipped choosing a printer the first time JusPrin started, it uses a stand-in, a generic 250 mm Klipper printer, until you add yours.

## Connect a printer

Connecting a printer lets JusPrin send prints to it and show how it is doing. JusPrin connects Bambu Lab printers, and printers that run Klipper with Moonraker or OctoPrint.

1. On Home, click **Connect…** on the printer's card, or open the card's menu (**Printer actions**) and choose **Connect…**.
2. The printer's chat asks for what it needs, such as its address. A Bambu Lab printer also needs its **Access code**, and a print host may need its **API key**. These stay on this computer.
3. **Help me find the code** explains where to find it on the printer.

A Bambu Lab printer needs Bambu's network plug-in. The chat says so when it is missing.

## Rename or remove a printer

Open the printer card's menu on Home (**Printer actions**):

- **Rename**, then type the new name under **Printer name** and click **Save**. A name cannot be empty, hold any of < > [ ] : / \ | ? * ", or be the name of another printer.
- **Remove printer…**, then **Remove**. The printer's own settings are deleted; your projects stay.
- **Printer settings…** and **Ask AI about printer settings…** open its settings.

## Bring printers from another slicer

In the **File** menu choose **Import**, then **Import from OrcaSlicer...** or **Import from JusPrin 1...**. The printers come with their filaments and print settings, and the other program keeps its own copy. JusPrin offers the same the first time it starts, when it finds them on the computer.

## Calibrate a printer or a filament

Calibration prints a small test, such as a temperature tower, and then sets the printer or filament from what the test shows.

1. Choose **Calibrate…** in the printer's menu, the **Printer** menu or the printer card's menu on Home, or **Calibrate this filament…** in the filament's menu.
2. A question names the printer and filament. Click **Start**. The open project is saved and closed, and the test opens as a project of its own, with a chat that asks which test to print.

Calibration needs AI. When it is not set up, the question offers **Set up AI…** instead of Start.

<!-- ai-description: Read before telling the person how to slice, check, send or export a print by hand, or where past prints are: the Slice and Print button and its menu, Check print, the print issues button on the 3D view with Ask AI and Ignore this warning, Export sliced file…, Print history, and print reports. -->

# Slicing, checking and printing

How to turn a project into a print: slice it, check it, and send it to the printer or save the file.

Names in bold are the words on screen. On a Mac the menus named here are in the menu bar. On Windows and Linux they are in the menu beside the **File** button in the title bar.

<!-- ai: These are the by-hand steps. I can slice and check a plate myself with my tools, and open the window that sends a print; the person always sends the print themselves. -->

## Slice and print

The button at the right of the header of the project does the next step for the plate you are working on:

- **Slice** while the plate is not sliced. Cmd+R on a Mac, Ctrl+R on Windows and Linux, does the same.
- **Slicing…** while it slices. The button beside it turns into an X, **Cancel slicing**, that stops it.
- **Print** once the plate is sliced, or **Print plate 2** and so on when the project has more plates. It opens the window that sends the print to the printer, where you start it. Switching to a plate that is not sliced brings **Slice** back.

The arrow beside the button (**Print actions**) has the other choices: **Slice all plates**, and once a plate is sliced, **Check Print**, **Print all plates…** and **Export sliced file…**. The **Print** menu has the same commands.

![The header of a sliced project, with Print plate 2 and the arrow beside it](pictures/slicing-and-printing/print-button.png)

When the printer is not connected, Print says **Printer connection required**: connect the printer first (the guide's page on printers describes it), or save the sliced file and print from a card.

## Check the print before printing

Choose **Check Print** in the menu beside the Print button, or **Check print…** in the **Print** menu. A window opens with the sliced plate and a report beside it.

- The report lists the print's **Time**, **Filament** and **Cost**, then what may need a look: **Supports**, **Seams**, **Slicer warnings**, **First layer**, **Unsupported islands**, **Crossing paths** and **Paths outside the plate**. When there is nothing to look at it says **Nothing to flag.**
- Click a finding to turn the view to it and show its layer.
- **Legend** shows what each colour of the sliced paths means.
- Close the window with the X at its top right or Escape. It also closes by itself when the plate changes and the slice is out of date.

![The Check print report for a plate with nothing to flag](pictures/slicing-and-printing/check-print.png)

## Print issues on the 3D view

When something about the plate would print badly or not at all, a button at the bottom right of the 3D view says how many issues there are, for example "2 print issues". Click it to see them. A bubble then points at the object each issue is about.

![A print issue's bubble beside its object, with Ask AI and Ignore this warning](pictures/slicing-and-printing/print-issue.png)

- **Ask AI** asks AI in the chat to explain the issue and what you can do about it.
- **Ignore this warning** stops counting a warning you have decided to live with. It stays in the list marked **Ignored**; open it there and click **Stop ignoring** to count it again. An issue that keeps the plate from printing cannot be ignored.
- The arrows in the bubble go to the next issue. The X, Escape, or a click on an empty part of the 3D view closes the bubble.

## Save the sliced file instead of sending it

Choose **Export sliced file…** in the menu beside the Print button, or in the **Print** menu, and pick where to save it. Take that file to the printer, for example on a memory card.

## Print history

<!-- ai-description: Read before explaining how the AI panel and its chats work or how AI is set up: New chat, the chats list, reopening an earlier chat, the model and thinking pickers, attaching files, credits, signing in to a JusPrin account, using your own API key, and connecting an outside AI tool. -->

# AI chats, account and credits

How to talk with AI about a project, and how to set up the AI it uses.

Names in bold are the words on screen. On a Mac the menus named here are in the menu bar. On Windows and Linux they are in the menu beside the **File** button in the title bar.

<!-- ai: This page is about me and how the person reaches me. When they ask what I can do, I answer from what I can do; these steps are for where things are on screen. -->

## The AI panel and its chats

The AI panel is at the right of an open project. If it is hidden, click the button at the right end of the header (**Show the AI panel**), or choose **Show AI panel** in the **View** menu (on Windows and Linux, tick **AI panel**).

Chats belong to the project they were started in, and are saved with it.

- **New chat**, the + at the top of the panel, starts a chat. It is greyed out while AI is replying.
- **Back to chats**, the arrow at the top left, shows the project's chats, newest first. Click one to open it.
- **Chat actions**, the "⋯" at the top, has **Rename** and **Delete**. Deleting a chat leaves the project and its print history as they are.
- Type in the box at the bottom and press Return to send; Shift+Return starts a new line. While AI replies, the send button becomes **Stop**.
- When AI ends a reply with choices, they show as buttons under it. Click one to answer with it, or type your own answer.

## Open an earlier chat

When the project has not changed since a chat's last turn, the chat simply opens and carries on.

When the project has changed since, the chat opens for reading only, with a note in place of the message box:

- **Restore and resume** puts the project back the way it was in that chat, then lets you carry on there. It asks first; what you have now stays in Version history.
- **Return to active chat** goes back to the chat you were in.
- **Ask current chat about this** quotes the earlier chat in your current one.

![An earlier chat opened for reading, with Restore and resume, Return to active chat and Ask current chat about this](pictures/ai-chats-and-account/earlier-chat.png)

## Choose the model and how hard it thinks

The two choices beside the message box set which AI model the chat uses and how long it thinks before answering. Models from a JusPrin account show how many credits a message costs.

A chat keeps the model and thinking it started with: both are locked once you send the first message. To use another model, start a new chat. To set the model new chats start with, open Preferences, then **BYOAI**, and choose under **New chats start with**.

## Attach a picture or a file

Click **Attach a file**, the + in the message box, and pick **Photo or image**, **3D model (STL, 3MF, STEP)**, **G-code** or **Document (PDF)**. You can also drop files on the message box or paste a picture. Each file shows as a row above the box, with **Remove** to take it off again.

A model that cannot see pictures says so on the picture's row, and the picture is not sent.

## Set up AI

With no AI set up, the panel says **No AI connected** and offers **Set up AI**, which opens Preferences on **Account**. There are three ways, and any of them works on its own:

- A JusPrin account: sign up, and JusPrin's own AI works with credits. See [Sign in](#sign-in-to-a-jusprin-account).
- Your own API key from an AI provider, billed by them. See [Your own API key](#use-your-own-api-key).
- An AI app you already use on this computer, which then works on the open project. See [Connect an AI tool](#connect-an-ai-tool-you-already-use).

To open Preferences: on a Mac choose **Preferences** in the JusPrin menu (Cmd+,); on Windows and Linux choose **Preferences** in the menu beside the **File** button (Ctrl+,). The "…" button at the right of the header also has **Preferences…**.

## Sign in to a JusPrin account

In Preferences, open **Account**.

- **Continue with Google** signs in through your browser. Come back to JusPrin when the browser says you are done.
- Or type your email address and click **Sign up free**, or **Sign in** for an account you have. JusPrin emails you a 6-digit code to type in. **Use a password instead** works for an account that has one.

![Preferences, Account, signed out, with Continue with Google and the email box](pictures/ai-chats-and-account/account.png)

Once signed in, Account shows the email address, the plan and the credits left, with **Get more credits**, **Billing and usage**, **Sign out** and **Delete account…**. Signing out keeps your projects, printers and API keys on this computer.

## Credits

With a JusPrin account, each message costs credits: the cheaper model costs fewer than the stronger one, and the model picker shows how many. A new account starts with free credits, and credits that run out soonest are spent first.

- The ring beside the model picker (**Credits left**) shows how many are left. Click it to see them, with **Get more credits** and **See usage**.
- When a message needs more credits than are left, the message box says so and offers **Get more credits**.

Your own API key and an outside AI tool use no credits.

## Use your own API key

1. In Preferences, open **BYOAI**.
2. Under **Your own API key**, click **Add key** beside Anthropic, OpenAI or OpenRouter, and paste the key.
3. Click **Check key**. JusPrin checks it with the provider and keeps it on this computer only. **Replace** and **Remove** change it later.

The provider bills you for what you use.

![Preferences, BYOAI, with the API key rows and the AI tools found on this computer](pictures/ai-chats-and-account/byoai.png)

## Connect an AI tool you already use

An AI app such as Claude Code or Codex can work on the project open in JusPrin.

1. In Preferences, open **BYOAI**. Under **Connect an AI tool you already use**, each tool says whether it was found on this computer. **Look again** searches again.
2. Click **Connect…** beside the tool. For some tools JusPrin shows a command to run, with **Copy**; for others it shows the change it will make to the tool's settings, and **Connect** makes it.
3. When it says **Connected**, click **Done**. The tool can now see and change the open project.

# The app itself

Where JusPrin's own preferences are, and the commands that are about the app rather than a project.

Names in bold are the words on screen. On a Mac the menus named here are in the menu bar. On Windows and Linux the **File** menu is the **File** button in the title bar, and the other menus are in the menu beside it.

<!-- ai: I cannot change these preferences myself; I give these steps. -->

## Open Preferences

- On a Mac, choose **Preferences** in the JusPrin menu, or press Cmd+,.
- On Windows and Linux, choose **Preferences** in the menu beside the **File** button, or press Ctrl+,.
- In a project, the "…" button at the right of the header has **Preferences…**. On Home, it is the gear button at the top right.

The window lists its sections at the left: **Account**, **BYOAI**, **Appearance**, **3D view**, **Projects & files** and **Updates**. Account and BYOAI set up AI; the guide's page on AI chats describes them. **More preferences…** at the bottom opens the app's full list of older preferences.

## Language, theme and units

In Preferences, open **Appearance**.

- **Language**: pick one from the list. JusPrin uses it after it restarts, and offers **Restart now** or **Later**. Restart now saves the project first.
- **Theme**: **Light** or **Dark**. The change shows at once.
- **Units**: **Millimetres** or **Inches**.

![Preferences, Appearance, with Language, Theme and Units](pictures/the-app/appearance.png)

## Mouse and touchpad in the 3D view

In Preferences, open **3D view**.

- **Controls**: **Mouse** or **Touchpad**, for how dragging and scrolling move the view.
- **Zoom toward the pointer** zooms to where the pointer is, instead of the middle of the view. **Reverse scroll-wheel zoom** turns the wheel's direction around. **Turn freely** lets the view turn past upside down.
- Under **Mouse buttons**, choose what **Left-drag**, **Middle-drag** and **Right-drag** do: **Turn the view**, **Pan** or **Nothing**.

The keys of the 3D view are listed under **Keyboard Shortcuts** in the **Help** menu.

![Preferences, 3D view, with the controls and what each mouse button does](pictures/the-app/3d-view.png)

## Show and hide the panels

An open project has a panel at the left, with the plates and the project, and the AI panel at the right.

- On a Mac, the **View** menu has **Show plates and project panel** and **Show AI panel**, which read **Hide…** while the panel is shown.
- On Windows and Linux, the **View** menu has **Plates and project panel** and **AI panel**, ticked while each is shown.
- The header has a button for each: at its far left for the plates panel, at its far right for the AI panel.
- **Home** in the **View** menu goes back to Home.

## Classic view

Classic view is the app's original screen, with all print settings in a panel at the side. Choose **Switch to classic view…** in the **View** menu, or in the "…" menu at the right of the header. To return, click **Back to JusPrin** on the bar across the top, or choose **Switch to JusPrin view** in the **View** menu.

## Updates

JusPrin looks for a newer version once a day, on GitHub. When there is one, **Updates** in Preferences is marked with a dot.

1. In Preferences, open **Updates**. **Check now** looks straight away.
2. When it says **JusPrin {v} is available** with the version, click **Download**. The release's page opens in your browser; download and install it from there.
3. **Skip this version** stops it asking about that version. **Release notes** shows what changed.

Untick **New JusPrin versions** to stop the daily check. The printer and filament profiles that come with JusPrin are updated with JusPrin itself.

![Preferences, Updates, with Check now and the choice of what to check for](pictures/the-app/updates.png)

## Report a problem or get help

- **Report a problem…** in the **Help** menu opens a new issue on JusPrin's GitHub page in your browser, with the app's version and your system already filled in. Nothing is sent until you submit it there.
- **JusPrin guide…** in the **Help** menu opens this guide inside the app, with a search box.
- **Ask AI…** in the **Help** menu opens the AI panel.
- **About JusPrin** shows the version, with **Copy version**, and how to get help. It is in the JusPrin menu on a Mac and in the **Help** menu on Windows and Linux.

## Quit

On a Mac, choose **Quit** in the JusPrin menu (Cmd+Q). On Windows choose **Exit** in the **File** menu, and on Linux **Quit** in the **File** menu.

![Print history, with an exported file and the Print again and Export… buttons](pictures/slicing-and-printing/print-history.png)

Each entry says where the file went and when, and whether the print finished. **Print again** sends the kept copy to the printer again, **Export…** saves it again, and **Open in chat** goes to the chat the print was made in. Type in **Search prints** to find one.

When you are signed in to a JusPrin account, an entry in Print history offers "Share how it printed and get 25 credits". It opens **Tell us how it printed**: add a photo with **Choose a photo…**, write what happened in at least 200 characters, say whether **It worked**, came out **Partly** or not, and click **Send report**. Each sliced file takes one report.

lines: - **OTHER PRINTERS**: click one to slice the project for that printer instead.
- **Printer settings…**, **Ask AI about printer settings…**, **Calibrate…** and **Add a printer…**.
+![The printer's menu, with the printer's state, Nozzle, Plate, the other printers and the settings commands](pictures/printers-and-filament/printer-menu.png)
When a project file brought its own printer, the printer is marked **From the file · not one of your printers**.
## Choose the filament and its colour
- **Remove printer…**, then **Remove**. The printer's own settings are deleted; your projects stay.
- **Printer settings…** and **Ask AI about printer settings…** open its settings.
+![A printer card on Home with its menu open](pictures/printers-and-filament/printer-card-menu.png)

In the **File** menu choose **Import**, then **Import from JusPrin 1**, or the item above it, which imports from the slicer JusPrin is built on. The printers come with their filaments and print settings, and the other program keeps its own copy. JusPrin offers the same the first time it starts, when it finds them on the computer.
Calibration prints a small test, such as a temperature tower, and then sets the printer or filament from what the test shows.
1. Choose **Calibrate…** in the printer's menu, the **Printer** menu or the printer card's menu on Home, or **Calibrate this filament…** in the filament's menu.

-- **Back to chats**, the arrow at the top left, shows the project's chats, newest first. Click one to open it.
+- **Back to chats**, the arrow at the top left, lists the project's chats. Click one to open it.
- **Chat actions**, the "⋯" at the top, has **Rename** and **Delete**. Deleting a chat leaves the project and its print history as they are.
- Type in the box at the bottom and press Return to send; Shift+Return starts a new line. While AI replies, the send button becomes **Stop**.
- When AI ends a reply with choices, they show as buttons under it. Click one to answer with it, or type your own answer.
- Click a plate to make it the plate you are working on. Only that plate is open in the list; a closed plate shows a short summary such as its object's name or how many objects it holds.
- Click an object to select it in the 3D view. Selecting an object in the 3D view selects it here too.
- A row may carry **Mesh needs repair**, **won't print**, the number of its filament, or "×2" and more for copies.
-- A diamond mark on a row means the plate or object has settings or painting of its own. Click it to see which.
+- A diamond mark on a row means the plate or object has settings or painting of its own. On an object, click it to see which; on a plate, it opens the plate's settings.
- **Arrange** to lay out the objects on this plate only.
- **Auto-orient** to turn this plate's objects to the side that prints best.
-- **Lock** to keep Arrange from moving this plate's objects. **Unlock** undoes it.
+- **Lock** to keep this plate's objects where they are. **Unlock** undoes it.
- **Plate settings…** for what can differ per plate, such as its bed type. The guide's page on print settings describes the window.
- **Move to front**, on plates after the first, to make it plate 1.
- **Delete plate**, when the plate can be deleted.
Cutting and painting have no button. With an object selected, press a key in the 3D view:
- C to cut the object in two.
-- L to paint where supports go, P to paint where seams go, N to paint colours on a multi-material print, H to paint fuzzy skin.
+- L to paint where supports go, P to paint where seams go, H to paint fuzzy skin.
- F to lay a chosen face flat on the plate.
-- T to add text on the object.
+The other keys of the 3D view are listed under **Keyboard Shortcuts** in the **Help** menu.
Each tool shows its own controls on the 3D view. Press Escape, or the same key, to close it.
- **Save** in the **File** menu (Cmd+S on a Mac, Ctrl+S on Windows and Linux) saves now and keeps that version for good, so it stays in Version history.
- An empty project is never saved. It is saved once it holds a model, and from then on even if you empty it.
- A project without a name takes the name of the first model in it.

-- If saving fails, for example because the disk is full, the "…" menu at the right of the header says **Changes couldn't be saved. JusPrin will retry.**, and saving starts again by itself once it can.

# Global Claude Code Rules

## How to Communicate

Talk like a colleague explaining something out loud, not like a report.

1. **Full sentences, one idea each.** Lead with a concrete case (someone opens a file, chats twenty times, then runs out of credits) before any general point. Never pack a mechanism into a noun phrase like "hidden fair-use ceiling". Say what the person sees happen, step by step.

2. **No labels of your own.** Names you made up while working ("phase 2", "board 6a", "the M4 batch", "the three decisions") mean nothing to me. Name a thing by what it is or does. To ask about a screen, say where it is and send the picture.

3. **Ask decisions in full, as questions.** Start with "Decision needed". Give one paragraph per decision: what it is, why it's mine, the options with what each costs, and your pick. End it with a "?". Never refer to a decision by a label, a count, or the report it's in. Don't hand me a choice you could settle yourself by searching or measuring.

4. **Mark proposals as proposals.** Keep apart what the code does today, what you propose, and what I have agreed to. Never write an idea I haven't approved as if it were settled. Before calling something "my rule", find my actual words.

5. **Report outcomes, not the journey.** Leave out problems you hit and solved unless they change what I do next. For an investigation, say what the problem was, how you solved it, what you tested and the result, and what's still open. Keep it under about 500 words.

## Git Commit Policy

When the user asks to commit changes:

1. Run `git status` and `git diff` to review the changes.
2. If you are confident that both the changes are correct and the proposed commit message accurately describes them, proceed with git commit without asking for confirmation.
3. If you have any uncertainty about either, stop and ask the user for explicit confirmation before committing.

When the user asks to revert or amend commits:
1. Explain what will be reverted/amended
2. Ask for confirmation before executing any `git revert`, `git reset`, or `git commit --amend` commands
3. Only proceed after explicit user approval
4. Never revert commits without explicit user confirmation.

This applies to all git operations that modify commit history.

## Submodule Policy

**Never commit or attempt to commit submodule updates.**

When `git status` shows modified submodules (e.g., `modified: some-submodule (new commits)`):
- Do not stage or commit the submodule change
- Do not include submodules when running `git add`
- Leave submodule management to the user

## Testing Principles

1. Always test your code change unless the change is not testable.

2. If the change is not testable, highlight the reason why it's not testable to get the user's attention.

3. By default, do end-to-end testing on everything that may potentially be impacted by your change on the local dev environment.

4. Search for how the dev environment should be started if it's not obvious.

5. Look for README files in the project for related info.

6. Check if the local dev is already running before you try to start it again.

## Software Engineering Principles

1. **Don't reinvent the wheel (avoid Not Invented Here).** Before building anything, check whether the codebase or the libraries it already uses do it, and reuse that. Re-implementing something is a decision that needs a stated justification.

## Where to Create Worktrees and Temporary Folders

This file is read by more than one coding tool, so each rule names the idea first and the tool-specific path second.

1. **Use the location your own tool already uses for worktrees.** Claude Code: `<repo>/.claude/worktrees/`. Codex: `~/.codex/worktrees/`. If this session was started inside a worktree the tool created, put any further worktree beside it.
2. **Never create a worktree or a working folder in `~` or directly under `~/Projects`.** That includes sibling folders such as `<repo>-worktrees`. This holds for a different repo than the one the session started in: use that repo's tool-managed location (rule 1) or the scratch directory (rule 3).
3. **Short-lived worktrees, build output, logs, screenshots and scripts go in the session's scratch or temp directory** if the tool gives one (Claude Code names it in the session instructions). If it gives none, use a new folder under the system temp directory, not the home directory.
4. **Keep non-worktree files out of worktree folders.** Logs, screenshots and scripts do not belong beside the worktrees. They go in the scratch directory, or inside the one worktree they concern.
5. **Use absolute paths when creating a worktree.** A shell may reset its working directory between commands, and a path starting with `~` or `..` can land somewhere unintended.
6. **Say where it is.** After creating a worktree, tell the user its full path, and remove it and its branch when the work is finished and merged.

## Bug Fix Policy

**Never apply a fix for a bug you cannot reproduce.**

Before writing any fix:
1. Reproduce the bug first in the local dev environment.
2. If the bug cannot be reproduced locally (e.g., only manifests in release mode, requires specific device conditions, or the debug framework masks the crash), stop and tell the user — do not apply the fix.
3. A fix is only valid if you can demonstrate the broken behavior before the fix and the correct behavior after.

## Epistemic Discipline — Root Cause of Repeated Errors

**The core failure mode: confusing "generating a plausible explanation" with "knowing the answer."**

Coherent ≠ true. A narrative that feels right because it's internally consistent is not a verified fact.

Rules to follow every time:

1. **Search before asserting, not after being challenged.** The internet is always available. Use it proactively, not reactively as damage control.

2. **Explicitly label inference vs. verified fact.** If it hasn't been confirmed by a source, say "my hypothesis is..." or "I'd expect..." — never state it as fact.

3. **"I don't know yet" is a complete and correct answer.** Saying it is more helpful than fabricating a confident-sounding explanation.

## Problem Definition Before Search

**A well-defined problem statement is more valuable than a clever hypothesis.**

The discipline:
1. **Define the problem precisely first.** Strip out assumptions one by one until the statement contains only what is actually known. Remove irrelevant context (e.g. subscription type if it doesn't affect the symptom).
2. **Search for the problem directly** — not for your hypothesis. People who already solved the same problem will surface the real root cause.
3. **Let the search results form the conclusion.** Don't search to confirm what you already believe.
4. **Be flexible about scope.** Start with the most likely affected area (e.g. Discord) but stay open to other channels or systems being equally or more affected.

Searching to validate a hypothesis finds confirmation of whatever you already believed. Searching for the problem finds answers.

## Upstream vs. fork attribution

This checkout holds two codebases: upstream OrcaSlicer (the `upstream` remote, SoftFever/OrcaSlicer) and the JusPrin fork's changes on top of it. Fork changes include everything under `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/` and the seams the fork added inside OrcaSlicer-owned files.

- Check before attributing; the file path is not enough. Run `git blame` on the line, then `git branch -r --contains <sha> 'upstream/*'`. No upstream branch containing the commit means the fork owns it. Run `git fetch upstream` first if the remote may be stale.

## Error handling discipline

- Do not catch an error merely because it can be caught. Catch only when the code can recover, translate the error at an abstraction boundary, or add context that is essential for diagnosis. Logging alone is not recovery.
- Represent expected states with normal control flow, not exceptions.
- Never turn an invariant violation or an "impossible" state into success or a silent no-op. Fix the invalid transition at the layer that owns the decision and let unexpected failures propagate to Sentry.
- Avoid duplicating defensive checks across layers. Keep lower-level operations strict, with their preconditions enforced by the caller that owns the workflow.
- If concurrency makes an invalid state reachable, fix the ordering or synchronization instead of suppressing the resulting error.
- Suppress an error only when it is genuinely expected and safely recoverable; document the reason and cover it with a test. Never broadly swallow unexpected errors.
- Prefer removing the root cause over reducing the visibility of its symptoms. Tests should encode valid transitions and assert that invalid ones remain visible.

### Building on a shared machine

Several agent sessions build on the same Mac at once. Without a limit, ninja runs one compile job per core plus two, so every build you start can take the whole machine. In 2026-10 one session stacked four builds in one build directory: 56 clang processes on 12 cores. It kept restarting its build to change targets and never limited the job count.

- Before starting a build, check `uptime` and `pgrep -fl ninja`. If the load is already above the core count, wait or build less.
- Limit jobs: `cmake --build … -- -j4`.
- Decide the full target list before starting. Never restart a running build to add or change targets: let it finish, then build the rest.
- Run one build per build directory. Two ninja processes in one directory compete and can leave its records inconsistent.
- Stopping a build means stopping ninja. `pkill -f "cmake --build …"` kills only the cmake wrapper, and ninja keeps compiling. Start long builds in their own process group (`perl -e 'setpgrp(0,0); exec @ARGV' cmake --build …`) and stop them with `kill -- -<pgid>`. Then confirm with `pgrep -fl ninja` before building again.
- When a build is slow, count your own compile processes before blaming the load on other sessions.
- Reuse an existing build where the task allows. Ask before configuring a fresh full-app build the task does not require.

## Code Style

- Wording: a file or object is "opened", "imported", "loaded" or "added", never "arrived". "Arrive" is fine for messages, responses, events and lists. `AgentUI/src/wording.test.ts` guards the text the model reads.
- Wording the model reads calls the product "the app", never Orca or OrcaSlicer: the model speaks as the app, and a second name reads as a second program. `AgentUI/src/wording.test.ts` guards this too. Log lines may name Orca. A throw may only if it never reaches the model: tool results forward save and open errors as they are, and the guard does not see those strings.

## Localization & translations

Catalogs live in `localization/i18n/<lang>/OrcaSlicer_<lang>.po`; the template is `OrcaSlicer.pot`.
See the [Localization guide](https://github.com/OrcaSlicer/OrcaSlicer_WIKI/blob/main/developer_reference/localization_guide.md) for the human-facing version of these principles.

### Writing translatable strings in the source

Translators see one msgid at a time and cannot change the code around it, so each message must be complete in a single msgid. Use the wrapper that fits instead of assembling text from pieces:

- **One msgid per sentence, with placeholders.** Never build a message by concatenating translated fragments (`_L("A") + name + _L(" is B")`) or by splicing a translated word such as `_L("left")` into another sentence: the translator can't reorder or inflect the parts. Write `format(_L("%1% is too close to others"), name)`.
- **A count needs a plural form.** Don't write `file(s)` or leave a verb unchanged after a number. Use `_L_PLURAL("%1% object", "%1% objects", n)`. libslic3r has no plural lookup, so word the message so it doesn't depend on a count, or build it in the GUI.
- **An ambiguous word needs a context.** When a short string means different things in different places (verb or noun, a mode name, a CAD term), give each sense its own context with `_L_CONTEXT`/`_u8L_CONTEXT`/`L_CONTEXT`. Keep the most common sense without a context so its existing translations stay valid.
- **Mark every user-visible string** (`_L`/`_u8L`, or `L` where it is translated later) and list new source files in `localization/i18n/list.txt`: files that aren't listed are never extracted.
- Add a `// TRN` comment above a new string whose meaning or placeholders aren't obvious.
- Never choose behavior by comparing translated text; compare ids or flags.

See `.claude/skills/orca-translations/references/source-audit.md` for the full checklist.

### Terminology

- Use the [Localization glossary](https://github.com/OrcaSlicer/OrcaSlicer_WIKI/blob/main/developer_reference/localization_glossary.md) as the source of truth for recurring terms, so the same English term is always rendered the same way within a language, and terms that must stay in English (brand/product names, acronyms, materials, file formats, G-code tokens, macros/variables/identifiers) are not translated.
- If a term's established translation changes, update both the affected `.po` files and the glossary (`developer_reference/glossary/<lang>.tsv` in the wiki, then regenerate) so they stay in sync.
- Translate the *meaning*, not the words. Check what the string actually controls before translating it — English reuses one word for different things. `Flow ratio` (multiplier), `Flow Rate` (throughput) and `Flow Dynamics` (pressure compensation) are three different terms; `extruder` may mean the toolhead, the feeder motor, or the nozzle depending on the string.
- Reuse one template per recurring message shape (`Failed to connect to …`, `Are you sure you want to …?`), even where the English wording varies.

### Editing rules

- Only edit `msgstr` — **never** change `msgid`, and never "fix" wrong English in the translation alone. Report the source string instead.
- Preserve exactly: placeholders (`%s`, `%d`, `%1%`, `%zu`, `%%`), every `\n` (count *and* position, including leading/trailing), leading/trailing spaces, HTML tags, `℃`, and the file's encoding and line endings.
- **Never reorder positional arguments** in a `c-format` string. If the msgid is `%d` then `%s`, that order must hold — swapping them breaks at runtime.
- `msgctxt` separates homonyms — always read it. `Back`/`Camera View` is the rear view of the 3D navigator, while `Back`/`Navigation` is the go-back button; `Top` exists in the *Alignment*, *Layers* and *Camera View* senses.
- When a string needs disambiguating, add context in the source (`_L_CONTEXT`/`_u8L_CONTEXT`), don't work around it in the translation.
- A literal `%` inside a string xgettext flagged `possible-c-format` will fail `msgfmt`. Fix it with a `// xgettext:no-c-format, no-boost-format` comment above the string in the source — do not mangle the translation or use `%%` in text that is never passed through printf.
- Plural entries: read `nplurals` from the catalog's `Plural-Forms` header (it is **not** always 2 — ja/ko/zh/th/vi use 1, ru/cs/pl/lt use 3, uk uses 4). Each form must be genuinely inflected for its quantity; repeating one sentence across all forms is a bug in Slavic/Baltic languages, though it is correct for Turkish and Hungarian.
- An entry whose `msgstr` equals its `msgid` is untranslated even though it is not empty; a plural entry with any empty form is likewise incomplete.
- Mark machine-produced translations with an `# AI Translated` translator comment. Don't add it to a human translation you didn't actually rewrite.
- When you can't be sure of a machine translation's meaning or UI wording, also add `# Needs human review: <what to check>`. Never use `fuzzy` for this — fuzzy entries are hidden from users.
- Don't reflow or re-wrap unrelated entries — keep the diff limited to the strings you changed.

### Verifying

- `scripts/run_gettext.bat --full` (Windows) regenerates the template, merges every catalog and compiles the `.mo` files. It must exit 0.
- Or check a single catalog with `msgfmt --check-format --check-header -o <out>.mo localization/i18n/<lang>/OrcaSlicer_<lang>.po`. Without `--check-header`, msgfmt skips the placeholder check in plural forms.
- Fuzzy entries are not shown to users. If you correct one, clear its `fuzzy` flag, otherwise the fix never ships.

# Global Claude Code Rules

## How to Communicate

Talk like a colleague explaining something out loud, not like a report.

1. **Full sentences, one idea each.** Lead with a concrete case (someone opens a file, chats twenty times, then runs out of credits) before any general point. Never pack a mechanism into a noun phrase like "hidden fair-use ceiling". Say what the person sees happen, step by step.

2. **No labels of your own.** Names you made up while working ("phase 2", "board 6a", "the M4 batch", "the three decisions") mean nothing to me. Name a thing by what it is or does. To ask about a screen, say where it is and send the picture.

3. **Ask decisions in full, as questions.** Start with "Decision needed". Give one paragraph per decision: what it is, why it's mine, the options with what each costs, and your pick. End it with a "?". Never refer to a decision by a label, a count, or the report it's in. Don't hand me a choice you could settle yourself by searching or measuring.

4. **Mark proposals as proposals.** Keep apart what the code does today, what you propose, and what I have agreed to. Never write an idea I haven't approved as if it were settled. Before calling something "my rule", find my actual words.

5. **Report outcomes, not the journey.** Leave out problems you hit and solved unless they change what I do next. For an investigation, say what the problem was, how you solved it, what you tested and the result, and what's still open. Keep it under about 500 words.

## Git Commit Policy

When the user asks to commit changes:

1. Run `git status` and `git diff` to review the changes.
2. If you are confident that both the changes are correct and the proposed commit message accurately describes them, proceed with git commit without asking for confirmation.
3. If you have any uncertainty about either, stop and ask the user for explicit confirmation before committing.

When the user asks to revert or amend commits:
1. Explain what will be reverted/amended
2. Ask for confirmation before executing any `git revert`, `git reset`, or `git commit --amend` commands
3. Only proceed after explicit user approval
4. Never revert commits without explicit user confirmation.

This applies to all git operations that modify commit history.

## Submodule Policy

**Never commit or attempt to commit submodule updates.**

When `git status` shows modified submodules (e.g., `modified: some-submodule (new commits)`):
- Do not stage or commit the submodule change
- Do not include submodules when running `git add`
- Leave submodule management to the user

## Testing Principles

1. Always test your code change unless the change is not testable.

2. If the change is not testable, highlight the reason why it's not testable to get the user's attention.

3. By default, do end-to-end testing on everything that may potentially be impacted by your change on the local dev environment.

4. Search for how the dev environment should be started if it's not obvious.

5. Look for README files in the project for related info.

6. Check if the local dev is already running before you try to start it again.

## Software Engineering Principles

1. **Don't reinvent the wheel (avoid Not Invented Here).** Before building anything, check whether the codebase or the libraries it already uses do it, and reuse that. Re-implementing something is a decision that needs a stated justification.

## Where to Create Worktrees and Temporary Folders

This file is read by more than one coding tool, so each rule names the idea first and the tool-specific path second.

1. **Use the location your own tool already uses for worktrees.** Claude Code: `<repo>/.claude/worktrees/`. Codex: `~/.codex/worktrees/`. If this session was started inside a worktree the tool created, put any further worktree beside it.
2. **Never create a worktree or a working folder in `~` or directly under `~/Projects`.** That includes sibling folders such as `<repo>-worktrees`. This holds for a different repo than the one the session started in: use that repo's tool-managed location (rule 1) or the scratch directory (rule 3).
3. **Short-lived worktrees, build output, logs, screenshots and scripts go in the session's scratch or temp directory** if the tool gives one (Claude Code names it in the session instructions). If it gives none, use a new folder under the system temp directory, not the home directory.
4. **Keep non-worktree files out of worktree folders.** Logs, screenshots and scripts do not belong beside the worktrees. They go in the scratch directory, or inside the one worktree they concern.
5. **Use absolute paths when creating a worktree.** A shell may reset its working directory between commands, and a path starting with `~` or `..` can land somewhere unintended.
6. **Say where it is.** After creating a worktree, tell the user its full path, and remove it and its branch when the work is finished and merged.

## Bug Fix Policy

**Never apply a fix for a bug you cannot reproduce.**

Before writing any fix:
1. Reproduce the bug first in the local dev environment.
2. If the bug cannot be reproduced locally (e.g., only manifests in release mode, requires specific device conditions, or the debug framework masks the crash), stop and tell the user — do not apply the fix.
3. A fix is only valid if you can demonstrate the broken behavior before the fix and the correct behavior after.

## Epistemic Discipline — Root Cause of Repeated Errors

**The core failure mode: confusing "generating a plausible explanation" with "knowing the answer."**

Coherent ≠ true. A narrative that feels right because it's internally consistent is not a verified fact.

Rules to follow every time:

1. **Search before asserting, not after being challenged.** The internet is always available. Use it proactively, not reactively as damage control.

2. **Explicitly label inference vs. verified fact.** If it hasn't been confirmed by a source, say "my hypothesis is..." or "I'd expect..." — never state it as fact.

3. **"I don't know yet" is a complete and correct answer.** Saying it is more helpful than fabricating a confident-sounding explanation.

## Problem Definition Before Search

**A well-defined problem statement is more valuable than a clever hypothesis.**

The discipline:
1. **Define the problem precisely first.** Strip out assumptions one by one until the statement contains only what is actually known. Remove irrelevant context (e.g. subscription type if it doesn't affect the symptom).
2. **Search for the problem directly** — not for your hypothesis. People who already solved the same problem will surface the real root cause.
3. **Let the search results form the conclusion.** Don't search to confirm what you already believe.
4. **Be flexible about scope.** Start with the most likely affected area (e.g. Discord) but stay open to other channels or systems being equally or more affected.

Searching to validate a hypothesis finds confirmation of whatever you already believed. Searching for the problem finds answers.

# CLAUDE.md

JusPrin — a long-lived fork of OrcaSlicer (open-source C++17 3D slicer, wxWidgets GUI, CMake build system).

## Upstream vs. fork attribution

This checkout holds two codebases: upstream OrcaSlicer (the `upstream` remote, SoftFever/OrcaSlicer) and the JusPrin fork's changes on top of it. Fork changes include everything under `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/` and the seams the fork added inside OrcaSlicer-owned files.

- Say "OrcaSlicer does X" only for behavior upstream ships. Behavior added by a fork commit is "JusPrin does X", even when it lives in an OrcaSlicer-owned file.
- Check before attributing; the file path is not enough. Run `git blame` on the line, then `git branch -r --contains <sha> 'upstream/*'`. No upstream branch containing the commit means the fork owns it. Run `git fetch upstream` first if the remote may be stale.
- If you have not checked, say it is unverified whether the behavior is upstream or fork.

## Branches

- `jusprin-dev` is the development branch. Start each change on a new branch from it and land the change there. It began at `975c703f08`, the merge of OrcaSlicer 2.5.0, and contains the earlier development branches `jusprin-newui` and `ui-walkthrough`; start nothing new on those.
- `main` is the stable branch and GitHub's default branch: the repository's front page, its issue forms, and the workflows GitHub runs on a schedule come from it.
  - Never force-push `main`, so that people who cloned the repository never have to force-pull. Only in an extreme case with no other way out, and with Kenneth's yes, may an admin lift the GitHub protection that blocks force pushes and deletion.
  - For now `main` is also the release branch: it moves forward from `jusprin-dev` when a version is released, and releases are built from it. This may change if a separate release branch is added later.
- `jusprin-v1` holds JusPrin 1, for fixes to that version only.
- `jusprin-v2-poc` holds the experiments described below.
- Take each OrcaSlicer release into `jusprin-dev` as `agent-docs/jusprin/fork-stewardship.md` rule 10 describes.

## Error handling discipline

- Do not catch an error merely because it can be caught. Catch only when the code can recover, translate the error at an abstraction boundary, or add context that is essential for diagnosis. Logging alone is not recovery.
- Represent expected states with normal control flow, not exceptions.
- Never turn an invariant violation or an "impossible" state into success or a silent no-op. Fix the invalid transition at the layer that owns the decision and let unexpected failures propagate to Sentry.
- Avoid duplicating defensive checks across layers. Keep lower-level operations strict, with their preconditions enforced by the caller that owns the workflow.
- If concurrency makes an invalid state reachable, fix the ordering or synchronization instead of suppressing the resulting error.
- Suppress an error only when it is genuinely expected and safely recoverable; document the reason and cover it with a test. Never broadly swallow unexpected errors.
- Prefer removing the root cause over reducing the visibility of its symptoms. Tests should encode valid transitions and assert that invalid ones remain visible.

## Build Commands

Build the Release configuration unless asked otherwise.

```bash
# macOS
cmake --build build/arm64 --config Release --target all --

# Linux
cmake --build build --config Release --target all --

# Windows
cmake --build . --config Release --target ALL_BUILD -- -m
```

Node/npm is required to build the Agent and Home pages, or configure with `-DJUSPRIN_BUILD_WEB=OFF` and supply the bundles.

### Building on a shared machine

Several agent sessions build on the same Mac at once. Without a limit, ninja runs one compile job per core plus two, so every build you start can take the whole machine. In 2026-10 one session stacked four builds in one build directory: 56 clang processes on 12 cores. It kept restarting its build to change targets and never limited the job count.

- Before starting a build, check `uptime` and `pgrep -fl ninja`. If the load is already above the core count, wait or build less.
- Limit jobs: `cmake --build … -- -j4`.
- Decide the full target list before starting. Never restart a running build to add or change targets: let it finish, then build the rest.
- Run one build per build directory. Two ninja processes in one directory compete and can leave its records inconsistent.
- Stopping a build means stopping ninja. `pkill -f "cmake --build …"` kills only the cmake wrapper, and ninja keeps compiling. Start long builds in their own process group (`perl -e 'setpgrp(0,0); exec @ARGV' cmake --build …`) and stop them with `kill -- -<pgid>`. Then confirm with `pgrep -fl ninja` before building again.
- When a build is slow, count your own compile processes before blaming the load on other sessions.
- Reuse an existing build where the task allows. Ask before configuring a fresh full-app build the task does not require.

## Testing

Catch2 framework. Tests in `tests/`; see [tests/AGENTS.md](tests/AGENTS.md) for where a new test belongs and the conventions to follow.

```bash
cd build && ctest -C Release --output-on-failure    # all tests
ctest --test-dir ./tests/libslic3r -C Release       # individual suite
ctest --test-dir ./tests/fff_print -C Release
```

Printer UI without hardware: `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Testing/README.md` (Bambu in-process fake); Moonraker and OctoPrint: `tests/printer_hosts/README.md` (Docker). Isolated `--datadir`; do not drive another JusPrin instance.

## Documentation

- Docs live in `docs/`; the high-level design of a subsystem goes in `docs/HLSD/<subsystem>.md`.
- Describe the design as it stands — what the subsystem does, why it exists, and the constraints that shape it. Not the route that got there: no phases, task lists, status markers, or "before/after this PR" framing.
- Planning and investigation output (brainstorms, superpowers design and plan docs) stays in `docs/superpowers/`, which is gitignored. Never commit it.
- Write a doc only when the design is not evident from the code, and when a change invalidates an existing one, update it in the same PR.
- The guide people and AI read is `docs/guide/`. Before a release, bring it in line with the app as `docs/guide/README.md` describes: run `scripts/check_guide.py`, fix every page it reports, and commit the pages with their pictures and skills.

## Code Style

- C++17, selective C++20. PascalCase classes, snake_case functions/variables
- `#pragma once` for headers. Smart pointers and RAII preferred
- Include what you use: include the header for every symbol a file uses, and keep headers compilable on their own. Never rely on the precompiled header or a transitive include. The `clang-tidy` CI job enforces this on changed lines; run the same check locally with `scripts/run_clang_tidy.sh` (`scripts\run_clang_tidy.ps1` on Windows), which sets up everything it needs
- Parallelization via TBB — be mindful of shared state
- Wording: a file or object is "opened", "imported", "loaded" or "added", never "arrived". "Arrive" is fine for messages, responses, events and lists. `AgentUI/src/wording.test.ts` guards the text the model reads.
- Wording the model reads calls the product "the app", never Orca or OrcaSlicer: the model speaks as the app, and a second name reads as a second program. `AgentUI/src/wording.test.ts` guards this too. Log lines may name Orca. A throw may only if it never reaches the model: tool results forward save and open errors as they are, and the guard does not see those strings.
- Always use `SetSizerAndFit(sizer)` instead of `SetSizer(sizer)` on top level window. Unless `SetSizer` must be called before the full layout is built, call `sizer->SetSizeHints(window)` afterwards in this case.

## Key Entry Points

- App startup: `src/OrcaSlicer.cpp`
- Slicing pipeline: `src/libslic3r/Print.cpp`
- All print/printer/material settings: `src/libslic3r/PrintConfig.cpp`

## Pull requests

Before opening a pull request or posting on GitHub, read [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md), including its "If you are an AI agent" section.

## Code review focus areas

- Changes must not cause regressions in existing functionality, defaults, profiles, or project compatibility.
- Features gated by options must not affect existing behavior when those options are disabled.
- Changes should follow the existing code style and architecture. Architectural changes should be justified in code comments and the PR description.
- Add helper functions or utilities only when existing code cannot reasonably be reused. Avoid duplication.
- Changes to OrcaSlicer-owned files must be additive where possible. Rewriting an upstream function, or reimplementing upstream behavior beside it, needs explicit justification in the PR description.
- When an upstream line is deleted or relocated, say where it went and what a future rebase must carry into the new home.
- Keep code concise and clear. Manually simplify AI generated bloated codes before review.
- Include targeted tests or documented verification for behavior changes, especially in slicing logic, profiles, formats, and GUI defaults.
- For profile changes (`resources/profiles/<Vendor>/**`), check that `version` in the sibling `resources/profiles/<Vendor>.json` was bumped.
- For new or changed UI strings, check they follow [Writing translatable strings in the source](#writing-translatable-strings-in-the-source): no concatenated fragments, plural forms for counts, contexts for ambiguous words.
- For translation changes (`localization/i18n/**/*.po`), check that recurring terms match the [Localization glossary](https://github.com/OrcaSlicer/OrcaSlicer_WIKI/blob/main/developer_reference/localization_glossary.md) for that language.

## Localization & translations

Catalogs live in `localization/i18n/<lang>/OrcaSlicer_<lang>.po`; the template is `OrcaSlicer.pot`.
See the [Localization guide](https://github.com/OrcaSlicer/OrcaSlicer_WIKI/blob/main/developer_reference/localization_guide.md) for the human-facing version of these principles.

### Writing translatable strings in the source

Translators see one msgid at a time and cannot change the code around it, so each message must be complete in a single msgid. Use the wrapper that fits instead of assembling text from pieces:

- **One msgid per sentence, with placeholders.** Never build a message by concatenating translated fragments (`_L("A") + name + _L(" is B")`) or by splicing a translated word such as `_L("left")` into another sentence: the translator can't reorder or inflect the parts. Write `format(_L("%1% is too close to others"), name)`.
- **A count needs a plural form.** Don't write `file(s)` or leave a verb unchanged after a number. Use `_L_PLURAL("%1% object", "%1% objects", n)`. libslic3r has no plural lookup, so word the message so it doesn't depend on a count, or build it in the GUI.
- **An ambiguous word needs a context.** When a short string means different things in different places (verb or noun, a mode name, a CAD term), give each sense its own context with `_L_CONTEXT`/`_u8L_CONTEXT`/`L_CONTEXT`. Keep the most common sense without a context so its existing translations stay valid.
- **Mark every user-visible string** (`_L`/`_u8L`, or `L` where it is translated later) and list new source files in `localization/i18n/list.txt`: files that aren't listed are never extracted.
- Add a `// TRN` comment above a new string whose meaning or placeholders aren't obvious.
- Never choose behavior by comparing translated text; compare ids or flags.

See `.claude/skills/orca-translations/references/source-audit.md` for the full checklist.

### Terminology

- Use the [Localization glossary](https://github.com/OrcaSlicer/OrcaSlicer_WIKI/blob/main/developer_reference/localization_glossary.md) as the source of truth for recurring terms, so the same English term is always rendered the same way within a language, and terms that must stay in English (brand/product names, acronyms, materials, file formats, G-code tokens, macros/variables/identifiers) are not translated.
- If a term's established translation changes, update both the affected `.po` files and the glossary (`developer_reference/glossary/<lang>.tsv` in the wiki, then regenerate) so they stay in sync.
- Translate the *meaning*, not the words. Check what the string actually controls before translating it — English reuses one word for different things. `Flow ratio` (multiplier), `Flow Rate` (throughput) and `Flow Dynamics` (pressure compensation) are three different terms; `extruder` may mean the toolhead, the feeder motor, or the nozzle depending on the string.
- Reuse one template per recurring message shape (`Failed to connect to …`, `Are you sure you want to …?`), even where the English wording varies.

### Editing rules

- Only edit `msgstr` — **never** change `msgid`, and never "fix" wrong English in the translation alone. Report the source string instead.
- Preserve exactly: placeholders (`%s`, `%d`, `%1%`, `%zu`, `%%`), every `\n` (count *and* position, including leading/trailing), leading/trailing spaces, HTML tags, `℃`, and the file's encoding and line endings.
- **Never reorder positional arguments** in a `c-format` string. If the msgid is `%d` then `%s`, that order must hold — swapping them breaks at runtime.
- `msgctxt` separates homonyms — always read it. `Back`/`Camera View` is the rear view of the 3D navigator, while `Back`/`Navigation` is the go-back button; `Top` exists in the *Alignment*, *Layers* and *Camera View* senses.
- When a string needs disambiguating, add context in the source (`_L_CONTEXT`/`_u8L_CONTEXT`), don't work around it in the translation.
- A literal `%` inside a string xgettext flagged `possible-c-format` will fail `msgfmt`. Fix it with a `// xgettext:no-c-format, no-boost-format` comment above the string in the source — do not mangle the translation or use `%%` in text that is never passed through printf.
- Plural entries: read `nplurals` from the catalog's `Plural-Forms` header (it is **not** always 2 — ja/ko/zh/th/vi use 1, ru/cs/pl/lt use 3, uk uses 4). Each form must be genuinely inflected for its quantity; repeating one sentence across all forms is a bug in Slavic/Baltic languages, though it is correct for Turkish and Hungarian.
- An entry whose `msgstr` equals its `msgid` is untranslated even though it is not empty; a plural entry with any empty form is likewise incomplete.
- Mark machine-produced translations with an `# AI Translated` translator comment. Don't add it to a human translation you didn't actually rewrite.
- When you can't be sure of a machine translation's meaning or UI wording, also add `# Needs human review: <what to check>`. Never use `fuzzy` for this — fuzzy entries are hidden from users.
- Don't reflow or re-wrap unrelated entries — keep the diff limited to the strings you changed.

### Verifying

- `scripts/run_gettext.bat --full` (Windows) regenerates the template, merges every catalog and compiles the `.mo` files. It must exit 0.
- Or check a single catalog with `msgfmt --check-format --check-header -o <out>.mo localization/i18n/<lang>/OrcaSlicer_<lang>.po`. Without `--check-header`, msgfmt skips the placeholder check in plural forms.
- Fuzzy entries are not shown to users. If you correct one, clear its `fuzzy` flag, otherwise the fix never ships.

Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:
   Another Claude Code session started this one; its brief is the task. Write the six guide pages still missing in `docs/guide`, each complete by the existing process, so that `scripts/check_guide.py --ask-ai` passes for all seven pages.

   The six areas below are a proposed split that Kenneth has seen but not explicitly approved. If the code shows a better boundary, say so and ask. Divide by what a person is trying to do, not by screen.
   1. Projects and files
   2. Plates and objects
   3. Printers and filament
   4. Slicing, checking and printing
   5. AI chats, account and credits
   6. The app itself

   Requirements for each page:
   - Write the steps from the code, never from `agent-docs/jusprin/product-definition.md`.
   - Quote on-screen labels exactly, in bold; the test checks each against the source.
   - Say where menus are on a Mac and on Windows and Linux.
   - Give every section a harness run in `tests/shell/guide_checks.json`, with named checks. Add the smallest harness mode or step where none exists.
   - Take the pictures via `tests/shell/run_guide_checks.py`, look at every picture, and correct the text where a picture shows it is wrong.
   - Add at least 3 questions to `tests/project_prompt/guide_questions.json`.
   - Add the page to the list in `docs/guide/README.md`.
   - The AI's copy is at most 16 KiB; the ai-description is at most 300 bytes. Make the seven descriptions distinct.
   - Text must not name OrcaSlicer, and calls the product "the app" (wording.test.ts).
   - Regenerate `tests/project_prompt/project_tools.json` with `JUSPRIN_UPDATE_PROJECT_TOOLS=1 agent_bridge_tests '[project]'`.

   Measure with `scripts/check_guide.py --ask-ai -- --backend claude-cli --judge claude-cli --claude-model claude-sonnet-5-5 --claude-judge-model claude-sonnet-5-5`, which runs on the Claude subscription and is approved. Report, per page, how many answers were right and whether the right guide was read. **Ask Kenneth before any paid run on another model.**

   Not part of this task: the Help window design, the system prompt, CI, merging, opening a PR. The live prompt suite must run before merge; name it as remaining and do not run a paid batch.

   Done looks like:
   - Seven pages, listed in the README.
   - Pictures from the built app, a harness run per section, and at least 3 questions per page.
   - check_guide --ask-ai passes.
   - These pass: the full AgentUI test suite, the type check, `agent_bridge_tests '[project]'`, and the prompt suite's unit tests.
   - The Help window shows all seven pages in the built app.

   Commit on my own branch. Report to Kenneth what was written, what was tested with results, which pictures are missing and why, and what is still open. His style: full sentences, no invented labels, proposals marked as proposals, decisions start "Decision needed", under ~500 words. The report's first 400 characters are relayed, so put what was done (the commit) first. If blocked, send ONE short question with SendMessage to `local_d51b4cef-a8f4-413a-9b3c-fe36d61dae7f`.

   Constraints from CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md:
   - Never commit submodules.
   - Never commit temp docs; leave them untracked and never ignore them.
   - Shared-machine build rules: -j4, one build per directory, check `uptime` and `pgrep -fl ninja`.
   - Run one harness at a time.
   - Use your own worktree and build dir only.
   - Do not put black pictures in a page.
   - Commit without asking only when confident; ask before revert, reset or amend.
   - Don't push or open a PR.

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   **Guide pages and their checks**
   - Each guide page starts with `<!-- ai-description: … -->`; `<!-- ai: … -->` holds notes only the AI gets.
   - A picture is a line of its own: `![alt](pictures/<page>/<name>.png)`. An indented picture line breaks the tests.
   - `guide.ts` builds `skills/guide-<area>/SKILL.md`. `guide.test.ts` checks labels with `hasLabel`: the label must appear in `src/slic3r/GUI/**/*.{cpp,hpp,ts,tsx}` (not `.test.` files) bounded by one of `"'`>` and `"'`<`.
   - `JUSPRIN_UPDATE_GUIDE_SKILLS=1` rewrites the skills.

   **run_guide_checks.py**
   - Entries have `covers`, `args` (`{dir}` is replaced), optional `env` (with `{dir}`), `checks`, and `pictures` (`"name": "file"`, or `{from, crop, atScreenSize}`).
   - With `checks`, the run stops once all named checks pass.
   - It refuses blank pictures and retries a failed run once.

   **Harness patterns** (tests/shell/shell_harness.cpp; mode docs at lines 6–~360)
   - `check(cond, name)` prints `HARNESS CHECK name PASS|FAIL`.
   - `capture_web_view(view, name)` (macOS WKWebView snapshot) gives good pictures.
   - `blit_screen` and `write_screen_capture` are screen grabs; they come out black without Screen Recording.
   - `snapshot_native_window(handle, path)` (harness_appearance.mm) draws a window's contentView, needs no screen grant, and gives 2x pictures.
   - `LeftPane::snapshot()` and `chip->snapshot()` give screen-size bitmaps (use `atScreenSize`).
   - Canvas GL readback (`glReadPixels`) gives the 3D view's own pixels.
   - Modal dialogs are handled with `answer_modals(id)` plus `m_modal_gate` (a lambda called every 200 ms; return false to keep the dialog open).
   - Text is read back from pages with the `document.title = '...'` trick via `WebView::RunScript`.
   - Waiting uses `wait_until(cond, name, then, each_tick)` and `wait_until_settled`.
   - `JUSPRIN_SOURCE_DIR` is defined for the harness.

   **Menus**
   - Mac: menu bar.
   - Windows and Linux: the File menu is the "File" button in the title bar (BBLTopbar). View, Print, Printer and Help are in the dropdown menu beside it.

   **Other**
   - `run_guide_tests.py` uses the recorded "advice-infill" point and answers skill_read with the asked guide. Its tool list comes from project_tools.json, which must be regenerated.

<!-- ai-description: Read before explaining how the AI panel and its chats work or how AI is set up: New chat, the chats list, reopening an earlier chat, the model and thinking pickers, attaching files, credits, signing in to a JusPrin account, using your own API key, and connecting an outside AI tool. -->

# AI chats, account and credits

How to talk with AI about a project, and how to set up the AI it uses.

Names in bold are the words on screen. On a Mac the menus named here are in the menu bar. On Windows and Linux they are in the menu beside the **File** button in the title bar.

<!-- ai: This page is about me and how the person reaches me. When they ask what I can do, I answer from what I can do; these steps are for where things are on screen. -->

## The AI panel and its chats

The AI panel is at the right of an open project. If it is hidden, click the button at the right end of the header (**Show the AI panel**), or choose **Show AI panel** in the **View** menu (on Windows and Linux, tick **AI panel**).

Chats belong to the project they were started in, and are saved with it.

- **New chat**, the + at the top of the panel, starts a chat. It is greyed out while AI is replying.
- **Back to chats**, the arrow at the top left, lists the project's chats. Click one to open it.
- **Chat actions**, the "⋯" at the top, has **Rename** and **Delete**. Deleting a chat leaves the project and its print history as they are.
- Type in the box at the bottom and press Return to send; Shift+Return starts a new line. While AI replies, the send button becomes **Stop**.
- When AI ends a reply with choices, they show as buttons under it. Click one to answer with it, or type your own answer.

## Open an earlier chat

When the project has not changed since a chat's last turn, the chat simply opens and carries on.

When the project has changed since, the chat opens for reading only, with a note in place of the message box:

- **Restore and resume** puts the project back the way it was in that chat, then lets you carry on there. It asks first; what you have now stays in Version history.
- **Return to active chat** goes back to the chat you were in.
- **Ask current chat about this** quotes the earlier chat in your current one.

![An earlier chat opened for reading, with Restore and resume, Return to active chat and Ask current chat about this](pictures/ai-chats-and-account/earlier-chat.png)

## Choose the model and how hard it thinks

The two choices beside the message box set which AI model the chat uses and how long it thinks before answering. Models from a JusPrin account show how many credits a message costs.

A chat keeps the model and thinking it started with: both are locked once you send the first message. To use another model, start a new chat. To set the model new chats start with, open Preferences, then **BYOAI**, and choose under **New chats start with**.

## Attach a picture or a file

Click **Attach a file**, the + in the message box, and pick **Photo or image**, **3D model (STL, 3MF, STEP)**, **G-code** or **Document (PDF)**. You can also drop files on the message box or paste a picture. Each file shows as a row above the box, with **Remove** to take it off again.

A model that cannot see pictures says so on the picture's row, and the picture is not sent.

## Set up AI

With no AI set up, the panel says **No AI connected** and offers **Set up AI**, which opens Preferences on **Account**. There are three ways, and any of them works on its own:

- A JusPrin account: sign up, and JusPrin's own AI works with credits. See [Sign in](#sign-in-to-a-jusprin-account).
- Your own API key from an AI provider, billed by them. See [Your own API key](#use-your-own-api-key).
- An AI app you already use on this computer, which then works on the open project. See [Connect an AI tool](#connect-an-ai-tool-you-already-use).

To open Preferences: on a Mac choose **Preferences** in the JusPrin menu (Cmd+,); on Windows and Linux choose **Preferences** in the menu beside the **File** button (Ctrl+,). The "…" button at the right of the header also has **Preferences…**.

## Sign in to a JusPrin account

In Preferences, open **Account**.

- **Continue with Google** signs in through your browser. Come back to JusPrin when the browser says you are done.
- Or type your email address and click **Sign up free**, or **Sign in** for an account you have. JusPrin emails you a 6-digit code to type in. **Use a password instead** works for an account that has one.

![Preferences, Account, signed out, with Continue with Google and the email box](pictures/ai-chats-and-account/account.png)

Once signed in, Account shows the email address, the plan and the credits left, with **Get more credits**, **Billing and usage**, **Sign out** and **Delete account…**. Signing out keeps your projects, printers and API keys on this computer.

## Credits

With a JusPrin account, each message costs credits: the cheaper model costs fewer than the stronger one, and the model picker shows how many. A new account starts with free credits, and credits that run out soonest are spent first.

- The ring beside the model picker (**Credits left**) shows how many are left. Click it to see them, with **Get more credits** and **See usage**.
- When a message needs more credits than are left, the message box says so and offers **Get more credits**.

Your own API key and an outside AI tool use no credits.

## Use your own API key

1. In Preferences, open **BYOAI**.
2. Under **Your own API key**, click **Add key** beside Anthropic, OpenAI or OpenRouter, and paste the key.
3. Click **Check key**. JusPrin checks it with the provider and keeps it on this computer only. **Replace** and **Remove** change it later.

The provider bills you for what you use.

![Preferences, BYOAI, with the API key rows and the AI tools found on this computer](pictures/ai-chats-and-account/byoai.png)

## Connect an AI tool you already use

An AI app such as Claude Code or Codex can work on the project open in JusPrin.

1. In Preferences, open **BYOAI**. Under **Connect an AI tool you already use**, each tool says whether it was found on this computer. **Look again** searches again.
2. Click **Connect…** beside the tool. For some tools JusPrin shows a command to run, with **Copy**; for others it shows the change it will make to the tool's settings, and **Connect** makes it.
