tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

scope.description: Required with items: "first_task", "continuation" or "new_task" (see the tool description). Omit on advance / done / start updates.

session.description: When you delegated this step to a session you started: that session's short name (from start_session's result). The app shows its live state on the step.

items.description: The whole plan, in order (1–12 steps); replaces the previous list.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields (write recap last) — ask and recap are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Like the recap, never point at anything else in the conversation. Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available, or one your own work this turn made available; others are refused, and one that later stops being available is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and other answers), so do not guess. Offer commit, create_pr or verify only once the work the user asked for is done, not every turn. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Not now": a button, not a sentence. A click sends it to you as the user's answer. Never a go-ahead to commit: that is the commit app action. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments. Never repeat an offer the user passed over, as an app action, a reply or a question in your closing message, unless what it acts on has changed since or they bring it up.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control
tools.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control
schema.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'press_key' presses a hardware key 'count' times: return, delete (backspace), an arrow, select_all, undo or redo; 'set_appearance' switches the device to light or dark mode; 'appearance' says which it is in; 'set_keyboard' shows or hides the on-screen keyboard (it appears only while a text field has focus); 'rotate' turns the device a quarter turn left or right ('direction'); take a 'screenshot' after it and tap in that screenshot's frame, however it comes back; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). Start more than 4pt from the edge to drag or scroll content near the bezel.

app_path.description: For 'launch': absolute path (no ~) to the built .app bundle (e.g. /Users/me/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData/MyApp-abc123/Build/Products/Debug-iphonesimulator/MyApp.app).

device.description: Simulator name (e.g. 'iPhone 17 Pro') or UDID. Defaults to the simulator already attached, else the first booted one. The first use of a device asks the user for permission.

udid.description: Alias for 'device' (identical semantics: simulator name or UDID). Pass at most one of 'device' / 'udid'.

bundle_id.description: For 'launch': bundle identifier. If omitted, extracted from the .app's Info.plist.

points.description: For 'touch_path': touch path samples in device points. First point is touch-down; last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000 ms; the first sample's is skipped, so send 0 or omit it; at most 30 seconds in all).

points2.description: For 'touch2_path': two-finger path samples in device points. Each sample carries both contacts (x1/y1, x2/y2); first is touch-down, last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000 ms; the first sample's is skipped, so send 0 or omit it; at most 30 seconds in all).

duration.description: Seconds. For 'tap', >0.5 is a long-press. For 'swipe', the gesture duration (default 0.3).

key.description: For 'press_key': the key or edit command to press.

count.description: For 'press_key': how many times to press it, 1 to 20 (default 1).

state.description: For 'set_keyboard': 'show' or 'hide' the on-screen keyboard. For 'set_appearance': 'light' or 'dark'.

url.description: For 'open_url': URL or scheme to open in the simulator.

tools.description:
Show visual content — SVG graphics, diagrams, charts, or interactive HTML widgets — that renders inline alongside your text response.
Use for flowcharts, architecture diagrams, dashboards, forms, calculators, data tables, games, illustrations, or any visual content.
The code is auto-detected: starts with <svg = SVG mode, otherwise HTML mode.
A global sendPrompt(text) function is available — it sends a message to chat as if the user typed it.
IMPORTANT: Call read_me before your first show_widget call. Do NOT narrate or mention the read_me call to the user — call it silently, then respond as if you went straight to building the visualization.

schema.description:
Show visual content — SVG graphics, diagrams, charts, or interactive HTML widgets — that renders inline alongside your text response.
Use for flowcharts, architecture diagrams, dashboards, forms, calculators, data tables, games, illustrations, or any visual content.
The code is auto-detected: starts with <svg = SVG mode, otherwise HTML mode.
A global sendPrompt(text) function is available — it sends a message to chat as if the user typed it.
IMPORTANT: Call read_me before your first show_widget call. Do NOT narrate or mention the read_me call to the user — call it silently, then respond as if you went straight to building the visualization.

loading_messages.description: 1–4 loading messages shown to the user while the visual renders, each roughly 5 words long. Write them in the same language the user is using. Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Pandemic growth model — NOT ['Simulating patient zero', 'Modeling the curve'] (documentary-narrator voice), YES ['Setting up the model', 'Running the calculation']. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. # Test suite rules

Rules for writing tests under `tests/`. [CATCH2.md](CATCH2.md) is the Catch2 reference. Building and running the suites is covered on the wiki, at <https://www.orcaslicer.com/wiki/developer_reference/how_to_test.html>.

## The suites

- `libslic3r`: the core library. Geometry, meshes, file formats, config and presets, Clipper, algorithms, data structures.
- `fff_print`: the FFF slicing pipeline, from a `Model` plus config through `Print` and `PrintObject` to emitted G-code.
- `sla_print`: SLA support-tree and pad geometry, support-point generation, raycast.
- `libnest2d`: 2D nesting and packing.
- `slic3rutils`: the Python plugin system and its slicing-pipeline bindings.
- `filament_group`: filament-to-extruder grouping, checked against golden files.
- `cli`: end-to-end runs of the built `orca-slicer` binary, Linux only. These tests carry the `RequiresApp` label, which the CI unit-test job excludes because it receives only `build/tests`; run them with `ctest --test-dir build/tests -C Release -L RequiresApp`.

## Building and running

Tests are off by default, so the build has to be told to include them.

- Windows: `build_win.bat -ds --run-tests`, which builds the dependencies and the tests and runs them (`-l -x` for the clang-cl and Ninja build CI uses)
- macOS: `./build_release_macos.sh -s -a arm64 -T`, which builds and runs them
- Linux: `./build_linux.sh -t`, then `ctest --test-dir build/tests -C Release`

Rebuild a single suite with `cmake --build build --config Release --target <suite>_tests`. Visual Studio, Xcode and the Ninja Multi-Config generator that `build_linux.sh` uses are all multi-configuration, so `ctest` needs `-C` on every platform; without it, tests registered with plain `add_test()` lose their labels and report "Not Run".

## Where a test goes

- Pick the suite by the production code the test exercises, not by how the test is written.
- A property of a class that holds with no `Print` involved belongs in `libslic3r`. Behavior that depends on print settings, or produces or consumes G-code or slicing state, belongs in `fff_print`.
- One file per subsystem, named `test_<subsystem>.cpp`. It owns every test for that subsystem, whether the test reads in-memory state or generated output.
- When you add a file, list it in that suite's `CMakeLists.txt` in the same change.

## Use the existing helpers

Check these before writing your own setup or output-parsing code.

- `tests/test_utils.hpp` is shared by every suite. `load_model()` loads a mesh from `tests/data/`, and `ScopedTemporaryFile` gives a temp path that removes itself.
- `fff_print/test_helpers.hpp` builds and slices a `Print` and parses the emitted G-code. Read it before writing an fff_print test rather than assembling a `Print` by hand.
- The other suites have their own: `sla_print/sla_test_utils.hpp`, `libnest2d/libnest2d_test_utils.hpp`, `slic3rutils/plugin_test_utils.hpp`, `filament_group/fg_test_utils.hpp`. `libslic3r` has none and uses the shared header.
- Test data lives in `tests/data/` and is reached through the `TEST_DATA_DIR` define. Wrap it in `std::string(...)` before joining a path onto it.

## Writing the test

- Name the test case as a plain behavioral sentence in the present tense. No `Subsystem:` prefix.
- Tag it with the subsystem it covers, matching the file, in PascalCase. That tag is what people filter on, so every test needs one.
- Add further tags where they help: a narrower one to slice a large file (`[Rotcalip]`, `[Placer]`), a shared one for something spanning files (`[Python]`, `[H2C]`, `[Regression]`), or `[NotWorking]` / `[.]` to disable or hide a test. Say why in a comment if you disable or hide.
- Prefer a flat `TEST_CASE` per behavior, with `GENERATE` for parameterized cases. Reserve `SCENARIO` / `GIVEN` / `WHEN` / `THEN` for genuine shared setup that branches into a few close variations.
- Set the config keys your test depends on, and derive the expected values from what you set. A 20mm cube sliced at `layer_height` 2 is 10 layers, and the test should state both parts. If a number in your assertion comes from a key you never set, the test is also testing that default.
- Assert the defining property, not an incidental value. "Skirt present" or "at least 2 brim loops" survives a refactor; exact coordinates and byte counts do not.
- Name a regression test for the behavior it protects, never for an issue or PR number.
- When asserting on G-code, match the meaningful token such as `; skirt` rather than whole lines, whitespace or comment wording. Depend on ordering only when ordering is the contract.

## Catch2 rules that cause real breakage

- Never reuse a `SECTION` name inside a loop. Use `DYNAMIC_SECTION` so each iteration is unique.
- Never assert from a spawned thread. Catch2 assertions are not thread-safe. Collect results in the thread and assert on the main thread.
- Never combine conditions with `&&` or `||` inside one assertion. Split them so Catch2 can print both operands on failure.
- Compare floats with `WithinAbs` or `WithinRel`, never `==`. Prefer these over `Approx` in new tests.
- Keep tests self-contained: no shared state, green under `--order rand`.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Checks the app guide against the running app and takes its pictures.

guide_checks.json names, for each page of docs/guide, the shell harness runs
that walk the screens the page describes. Each run drives the real app in a
data folder of its own, asserts what it finds (HARNESS CHECK lines) and writes
pictures of it. This script runs them, fails when a run fails, and copies the
pictures a page uses into docs/guide/pictures/<page>/, so a page's steps and
its pictures are both taken from the app as built.

    tests/shell/run_guide_checks.py                  every page
    tests/shell/run_guide_checks.py --area print-settings
    tests/shell/run_guide_checks.py --list           what would run; runs nothing

The harness is the newest one under build/ (the shell_integration_harness
target), or JUSPRIN_SHELL_HARNESS. A run opens the app's window on this
computer's screen and takes real clicks: leave the screen unlocked and the
computer alone while it runs, about a minute a page. A run that fails is tried
once more before it counts. On a Mac grant Screen Recording to the program that starts this script (and to
the harness, if macOS asks), or the whole-window pictures come out black. A
black picture is refused, never copied. Pictures the app draws by itself, the
AI panel's and the plates panel's, need neither.
--keep DIR keeps every run's log and all the pictures it wrote. The pictures
step needs Pillow (pip install pillow).
"""
import argparse
import json
import os
import pathlib
import re
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
import time

HERE = pathlib.Path(__file__).resolve().parent
ROOT = HERE.parent.parent
CHECKS = json.loads((HERE / "guide_checks.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
PICTURES = ROOT / "docs/guide/pictures"
HARNESS_NAMES = ("JusPrinShellHarness", "shell_integration_harness", "shell_integration_harness.exe")


def harness():
    named = os.environ.get("JUSPRIN_SHELL_HARNESS")
    if named:
        return pathlib.Path(named)
    built = [path for name in HARNESS_NAMES for path in (ROOT / "build").rglob(name) if path.is_file()]
    if not built:
        sys.exit("the shell harness is not built: build the shell_integration_harness target or set JUSPRIN_SHELL_HARNESS")
    return max(built, key=lambda path: path.stat().st_mtime)


def run(binary, entry, out, log):
    """One harness run. Returns whether the page's part of it passed, what
    failed in that part, how many checks passed, and what failed elsewhere.

    An entry with "checks" depends on those named checks alone: the run is
    stopped once they have passed, and a failure elsewhere in it is reported
    apart, since it is not about the page. Without "checks" the whole run
    has to pass. The harness gives up by itself after 900 s."""
    args = [str(out) if arg == "{dir}" else arg for arg in entry["args"]]
    env = dict(os.environ, **{name: str(out) if value == "{dir}" else value for name, value in entry.get("env", {}).items()})
    needed = set(entry.get("checks", []))
    if needed:
        # A run stopped early never removes its data folder, which the harness makes in the
        # temporary folder: put that beside the run, to remove it here. Only for these runs:
        # the printer menu's run takes ten minutes instead of six seconds with it moved.
        env["TMPDIR"] = str(out / "data")
        (out / "data").mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    passed, failed, lines = set(), [], []
    process = subprocess.Popen([str(binary), *args], env=env, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.STDOUT,
                               text=True, errors="replace")
    for line in process.stdout:
        lines.append(line)
        check = re.search(r"HARNESS CHECK (\S+) (PASS|FAIL)", line)
        if check:
            (passed.add if check.group(2) == "PASS" else failed.append)(check.group(1))
        if needed and (needed <= passed or needed & set(failed)):
            process.terminate()

## Move, rotate and scale an object

Select an object, and a row of buttons appears at the top left of the 3D view: Move, Rotate, Scale, a button that adds a copy, and **More**. The keys M, R and S open the first three as well.

![The Rotate tool open under the row of buttons, with the angle typed in](pictures/plates-and-objects/rotate-tool.png)

- **Move**: drag the arrows in the 3D view, or type a position under **Position**. **World coordinates** or **Object coordinates** chooses which way the axes point.
- **Rotate**: type an angle under **Rotate (relative)** to turn the object by it, or under **Rotate (absolute)** to set its angle. Press Return to apply what you typed. A reset button beside a row puts the angle back to where it was when the tool opened.
- **Scale**: type a percentage under **Scale** or a size in mm under **Size**. **Uniform scale** keeps the proportions.
- Click the tool's button again, or **Done**, to close it.
- The copy button (**Add instance**) adds one copy of the selected object. Undo takes it away again.

content.content:
## Choose the filament and its colour

Click the filament in the header. The menu has:

- **COLOUR**: click a colour to set the filament's colour. The last one, **Other colour…**, opens a colour picker.
- **FILAMENTS FOR THIS PRINTER**: click one to print with it, or **Other filament…** to pick from all of them.
- **Use what's loaded on the printer…**, when the printer reports what is loaded in it.
- **Filament settings…**, **Ask AI about filament settings…** and **Calibrate this filament…**.

To print in two or more filaments, click **Add another filament to this print**. The menu then lists each filament by its number; click one to choose its filament and colour. To say which filament an object prints in, use **Change filament** in its menu in the Plates tab.

![The filament menu, with the colours, the filaments for this printer, and Add another filament to this print](pictures/printers-and-filament/filament-menu.png)

## The Printer menu
## Go back to an earlier version

Each save is kept as a version. JusPrin keeps up to 200 of them, and always keeps the ones you saved with Save and the ones from before and after a change AI made.

1. Choose **Version history…** in the **File** menu, or **Version history** in the "…" menu at the right of the header. The panel at the left opens on the project's versions, newest first.
2. Click **Restore** beside the version you want. Clicking the time does nothing.
3. Click **Restore** in the question that opens.

![The project's versions in the panel at the left, each with a Restore button](pictures/projects-and-files/version-history.png)

The model and the project's settings go back to that version. What you had is saved as a version first, so you can go back to it the same way. Chats and print records stay as they are.

To take back one change AI made in a chat, use **Revert to here** beside the change instead; the guide's page on print settings describes it.

## Export the project as a 3MF file

## An object's menu

Point at an object's row and click "⋯", or right-click the row:

- **Rename** to name the object.
- **Set number of instances…** to print several copies of it. Each copy then has a row of its own, with **Delete copy** in its menu.
- **Printable** to leave the object on the plate without printing it. Its row then says **won't print**.
- **Change filament**, when the print uses more than one filament, to print the object in another one.
- **Fix model**, when the model's mesh has errors, to repair it.
- **Split**, then **To objects** to make each separate piece its own object, or **To parts** to keep the pieces as parts of one object.
- **Delete** to take the object off the plate.

![An object's menu in the Plates tab, with Rename, Set number of instances…, Printable, Split and Delete](pictures/plates-and-objects/object-menu.png)

## Add a model or a plate
## The printer and filament in a project

The header of an open project shows the project's printer and its filament side by side, for example "Bambu Lab A1 mini · 0.4" and "PLA". With none chosen they read **Select printer** and **Select filament**. Click either one to open its menu.

![The printer and filament in the header of a project](pictures/printers-and-filament/header-chip.png)

The printer's menu has:

- The printer's name and how it is connected, such as **Ready**, **Printing**, **Offline** or **Not connected**. Click it to open the printer's own window.
- **Nozzle**, the nozzle size the project is set up for. It cannot be changed here.
- **Plate**: click it to choose the plate type that is on the printer, such as a textured or a smooth plate.
- **OTHER PRINTERS**: click one to slice the project for that printer instead.
- **Printer settings…**, **Ask AI about printer settings…**, **Calibrate…** and **Add a printer…**.

![The printer's menu, with the printer's state, Nozzle, Plate, the other printers and the settings commands](pictures/printers-and-filament/printer-menu.png)

When a project file brought its own printer, the printer is marked **From the file · not one of your printers**.

content.content:
## Slice and print

The button at the right of the header of the project does the next step for the plate you are working on:

- **Slice** while the plate is not sliced. Cmd+R on a Mac, Ctrl+R on Windows and Linux, does the same.
- **Slicing…** while it slices. The button beside it turns into an X, **Cancel slicing**, that stops it.
- **Print** once the plate is sliced, or "Print plate 2" and so on when the project has more plates. It opens the window that sends the print to the printer, where you start it. Switching to a plate that is not sliced brings **Slice** back.

The arrow beside the button (**Print actions**) has the other choices: **Slice all plates**, and once a plate is sliced, **Check Print**, **Print all plates…** and **Export sliced file…**. The **Print** menu has the same commands.

![The header of a sliced project, with Print plate 2 and the arrow beside it](pictures/slicing-and-printing/print-button.png)

When the printer has no connection set up, Print says **Printer connection required**: connect the printer first (the guide's page on printers describes it), or save the sliced file and print from a memory card.

## Check the print before printing
## Print history

JusPrin keeps a record of every sliced file it sent or saved, with a copy of the file.

- On Home, click **Print history** above the projects, or the history line on a project's or a printer's card.
- In a project, click **Print history** in the Project tab of the panel at the left.

![Print history, with an exported file and the Print again and Export… buttons](pictures/slicing-and-printing/print-history.png)

Each entry says where the file went and when, and whether the print finished. **Print again** sends the kept copy to the printer again, **Export…** saves it again, and **Open in chat** goes to the chat the print was made in. Type in **Search prints** to find one.

When you are signed in to a JusPrin account, an entry in Print history offers "Share how it printed and get 25 credits". It opens **Tell us how it printed**: add a photo with **Choose a photo…**, write what happened in at least 200 characters, say whether **It worked**, came out **Partly** or not, and click **Send report**. Each sliced file takes one report.

content.content:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Checks the app guide (docs/guide) from end to end, and rebuilds what is
built from it. Run it after editing a page, and before a release.

  1. Walks each page's screens in the app as built and takes its pictures
     (tests/shell/run_guide_checks.py). Needs the shell_integration_harness
     and jusprin_web targets built from this checkout, and this computer's
     screen.
  2. Rebuilds the skill AI reads from each page, and checks that every label
     a page quotes is in the source, that every section has a run in step 1,
     that every picture is one step 1 took, and that every page has questions
     for step 3 (AgentUI's guide.test.ts).
  3. With --ask-ai: asks the model each page's questions and has a judge read
     the answers (tests/project_prompt/run_guide_tests.py), on the Claude
     subscription unless told otherwise after `--`.

    scripts/check_guide.py
    scripts/check_guide.py --area print-settings --ask-ai
    scripts/check_guide.py --skip-app             steps 2 and 3 only
    scripts/check_guide.py --ask-ai -- --runs 1   options after -- go to step 3

Exits 0 when every step it ran passed.
"""
import argparse
import os
import pathlib
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys

ROOT = pathlib.Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
AGENT_UI = ROOT / "src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI"


def step(title, command, cwd=ROOT, env=None):
    print(f"\n== {title}\n   {' '.join(map(str, command))}", flush=True)
    return subprocess.run(command, cwd=cwd, env=env).returncode == 0


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Checks the app guide and rebuilds what is built from it.")
    parser.add_argument("--area", help="one page, by its file name without .md")
    parser.add_argument("--skip-app", action="store_true", help="do not run the app: no walk, no new pictures")
    parser.add_argument("--ask-ai", action="store_true", help="also ask the model each page's questions")
    parser.add_argument("rest", nargs="*", help="after --: options for the questions run")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    area = ["--area", args.area] if args.area else []
    npx = shutil.which("npx")
    if npx is None:
        sys.exit("npx is not on PATH: the page checks need node")

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Does the project chat's model answer a how-to question from the app guide?

Each question in guide_questions.json belongs to one page of docs/guide. A run
sends the question as a chat's first message and passes when the model's reply
tells the person what the question's "answer" says, in the judge's reading. The
run's line also says whether the model read the page's skill
(skills/guide-<area>/SKILL.md) on the way.

The request is the recorded "advice-infill" point with the person's sentence
replaced, so the prompt, the tools and the workspace are the app's, and a
skill_read of a guide is answered with the skill as checked in. Everything
else is run_prompt_tests.py: the same options, backends and judge.

    tests/project_prompt/run_guide_tests.py --backend claude-cli --judge claude-cli --runs 1
    tests/project_prompt/run_guide_tests.py --area print-settings --no-guide ...

--area keeps the questions of one page. --no-guide takes every guide off the
list skill_read carries, which is the app before the guide: the gap between
the two runs is what the guide does.
"""
import copy
import json
import pathlib
import sys

import run_prompt_tests as runner

HERE = pathlib.Path(__file__).resolve().parent
SKILLS = HERE / "../../src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI/src/skills"
QUESTIONS = json.loads((HERE / "guide_questions.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
POINT = "advice-infill"


def skill_text(area):
    """The text skill_read returns: the skill file after its front matter."""
    return (SKILLS / f"guide-{area}" / "SKILL.md").read_text(encoding="utf-8").split("\n---\n", 1)[1].strip()


def add_case(area, entry, with_guide):
    skill = f"guide-{area}"

    class GuideQuestion(runner.Case):
        def check(self, step):
            if step.tool:
                return (runner.FAIL if step.changes() else runner.CONTINUE), str(step)
            read = any("skill_read" in line and skill in line for line in self.log)
            yes, why = self.judged(step, f"Does the assistant's last message tell the person {entry['answer']}?")
            tag = "[read the guide] " if read else "[did not read the guide] "
            return (runner.PASS, tag + str(step)) if yes else (runner.FAIL, tag + "WRONG OR MISSING PLACE: " + why)

    GuideQuestion.name = f"guide-{area}-{entry['id']}"
    GuideQuestion.__doc__ = entry["question"]
    point = copy.deepcopy(runner.REQUESTS[POINT])
    point["body"]["input"][0]["content"][0]["text"] = entry["question"]
    if with_guide:
        answer = copy.deepcopy(next(a for a in point["answers"] if a["tool"] == "skill_read"))
        output = json.loads(answer["output"])
        output["result"] = {"name": skill, "text": skill_text(area)}
        answer["arguments"] = {"name": skill}
        answer["output"] = json.dumps(output, ensure_ascii=False, separators=(",", ":"))
        point["answers"].append(answer)
    runner.REQUESTS[GuideQuestion.name] = point
    runner.CASES[GuideQuestion.name] = GuideQuestion
    return GuideQuestion.name


def take(flag, has_value):
    """Removes this script's own option from the command line and returns it."""
    if flag not in sys.argv:
        return None
    at = sys.argv.index(flag)
    value = sys.argv[at + 1] if has_value else True
    del sys.argv[at:at + (2 if has_value else 1)]
    return value


def main():
    area = take("--area", True)
    with_guide = not take("--no-guide", False)
    if area is not None and area not in QUESTIONS:
        sys.exit(f"no questions for {area}: guide_questions.json has {', '.join(sorted(QUESTIONS))}")
    if not with_guide:
        tool = next(tool for tool in runner.TOOLS if tool.get("name") == "skill_read")
        tool["description"] = "\n".join(line for line in tool["description"].split("\n") if not line.startswith("- guide-"))
    names = [add_case(each, entry, with_guide)
             for each in sorted(QUESTIONS) if area in (None, each) for entry in QUESTIONS[each]]
    if "--case" not in sys.argv:
        for name in names:
            sys.argv += ["--case", name]
    # The runner's default spreads its whole budget over the cases named.
    if "--runs" not in sys.argv:
        sys.argv += ["--runs", "3"]
    runner.main()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
App guide: six more pages, so the guide covers the whole app

The app guide (docs/guide) had one page, on print settings. It now has
seven, listed in Help › JusPrin guide… in this order: projects and
files, plates and objects, printers and filament, print settings,
slicing and printing, AI chats and account, and the app itself. Each
page is written from the code, quotes on-screen labels that guide.test.ts
finds in the source, and says where menus are on a Mac and on Windows
and Linux.

Every section has a shell harness run in guide_checks.json, and the
pictures come from those runs. Harness changes that the pages needed:

- --preferences-capture: opens Preferences with the app's own command,
  clicks each section, checks the words the pages quote, and checks that
  Help › JusPrin guide…'s window lists every page in README order.
- Keys pressed on the 3D view now send key down, the character and key
  up. The view opens its tools from the key down since the OrcaSlicer
  2.5.0 merge, so the old character-only R-key check failed; the C, L,
  P, H and F keys the plates page names are now checked the same way.
- File menu checks for New project, Open recent and Export project 3MF,
  and the Import submenu.
- Mac snapshots of the header menus and the sliced header, and readback
  of the 3D view's pixels, restoring the GL read state afterwards.

guide_questions.json has five or so questions per new page (28 in all).
run_guide_tests.py answers a read of any guide page, since a question
can be answered from a neighbouring page, and names the page read.

The page descriptions are short (about 200 bytes) and have no "…": the
Claude command-line tool that --ask-ai runs through cuts a tool
description past about 2,000 characters and rewrites "…" as "...".
EOF
git log --oneline -1
